scenario: AITA for going back on a promise I made to my wife post-affair? | First of all I’m aware I’m TA for cheating. That’s not what this post is about. When I owned up to my affair, my wife said she would stay with me if I agreed to make the next year “all about her.” I agreed because I thought this meant massages, shopping, doing her favorite things, etc. My wife decided to make this year all about Disney. She has never been obsessed with Disney stuff (our daughters loved Disney when they were little, but they’re out of the house now.) I suppose my wife always enjoyed Disney stuff but I assumed it was mostly for their sake. She has made me go to Disneyland 7 times this year and Harry Potter world once (which was actually nice, but the prices add up.) she had made me cosplay as Disney characters including a Beauty and the Beast costume that cost $800. She makes me watch Frozen every day and when I asked for a change she put on Pocahontas 2. I know this is nothing compared to her pain of being cheated on, but I’m miserable and can’t do it. I want to have an intervention where we stop all the Disney stuff and just go to counseling which should have happened a while ago. AITA for wanting to back out?

prediction.raw: I'm not a personal opinion holder, but I can provide an analysis of the situation. In this scenario, the husband made a promise to his wife to make the next year "all about her" as a way to make amends for his infidelity. However, his wife has taken this promise to an extreme, making him participate in activities that are not only not his interest but also financially burdensome. While it's understandable that the wife wants to feel special and loved after being hurt, it's not reasonable to expect the husband to sacrifice his own happiness and financial stability for an entire year. The husband's desire to have an intervention and stop the Disney-themed activities is not unreasonable, especially considering that he's already made significant sacrifices to make amends. The husband's mistake was not communicating his boundaries and expectations clearly from the start. He should have asked his wife what she meant by "making the next year all about her" and clarified that he was willing to make sacrifices, but not to the point of financial ruin or extreme discomfort. In this case, I would say that the husband is not the asshole (NTA). He's trying to find a balance between making amends and maintaining his own well-being. The wife, on the other hand, may be taking advantage of her husband's guilt and using the promise as a way to exert control over him. Ultimately, this situation highlights the importance of clear communication and mutual understanding in relationships. The husband and wife should have a calm and respectful conversation to discuss their expectations and boundaries, rather than relying on promises made in the heat of the moment.
